cards.title: Tell me about dogs
cards.body:
Type "Tell me about dogs" into a chatbot and you'll get a long, general essay: breeds, history, care. Probably not what you needed.

Type "I'm 12 and getting my first puppy. Give me 5 tips for the first week, one sentence each" and you get exactly that.

Same chatbot. The difference is what you asked.

cards.title: What a good prompt says
cards.body:
What you type to a chatbot is called a **prompt**. Remember, it writes the likely next words for **your** text, so the more your prompt says, the better it can aim. A good prompt usually says:

- **The goal:** what you want (explain, list, check, brainstorm).
- **The context:** who it's for and what you already know or have ("I'm 12", "here are my notes").
- **The format:** how long, and what shape (3 sentences, a list of 5, a table).

Being specific beats being long: one clear sentence can do more than a paragraph of waffle.

cards.prompt: Is each prompt **vague**, or **clear** about what it wants and what shape?

items.label: Tell me all about rivers, please!

cards.hint: For each one, ask: does it say what it wants, who it's for, and how long or what shape?
cards.nudge: A long or polite prompt can still be vague. Look for the ones that say exactly what they want and what shape.
cards.explanation: The clear ones say the **goal** (explain, titles) and the **format** (3 sentences, 3 titles), and the robot one gives context. "Tell me all about rivers, please!" is polite, but still vague: all of what, for whom, how long?

cards.prompt: Your prompt is: **"Write a summary of the water cycle."** It has a goal. What would improve it **most**?

options.text: Saying who it's for and how long it should be

options.nudge: Being polite is nice, but what information is still missing?
"Lots of detail" makes it longer, not better aimed. Who is it for, and how long should it be?
Everyone wants it good. What would actually help it aim the answer?

cards.hint: Check it against the three parts of a good prompt. Which two are missing?
cards.explanation: It has a **goal**, but no **context** (who's it for? a 12-year-old? a science test?) and no **format** (one paragraph? five bullet points?). Adding those does far more than politeness, capitals or repeating yourself.

cards.prompt: These bits are from different prompts. Is each one the **goal**, the **context** or the **format**?
cards.hint: Goal = what you want done. Context = who it's for, or what you already know or have. Format = the shape or length of the answer.
cards.nudge: "For my little brother" changes who it's aimed at, and "I've already read chapter 1" is something you know. What kind of part are those?
cards.explanation: **Goals** say what to do (summarise, explain). **Context** says who it's for or what you already know (your little brother, chapter 1). **Format** is the shape (a rhyme, a table).

cards.prompt: You're preparing a 1-minute talk about octopuses for class.

steps.text: You type "octopus facts". The chatbot replies with 20 long paragraphs. What do you change?

choices.consequence: You get another 20 paragraphs, a bit different. Nothing you said changed, so nothing useful changed.

choices.text: "3 surprising octopus facts for a 1-minute talk, one sentence each"
choices.consequence: Much better: three short, surprising facts. One says an octopus has "nine brains".

choices.text: Turn the temperature right up for more interesting facts
choices.consequence: The facts get stranger, and some make no sense. Temperature changes how it picks, not what it knows.

steps.text: "Nine brains" sounds amazing. What do you do before using it?

choices.text: Check it on a trusted science website
choices.consequence: It's close: an octopus has one central brain plus a cluster of nerve cells in each of its 8 arms, so you say that.

choices.text: Use it: it's from a good prompt
choices.consequence: A good prompt gets a better-aimed answer, not a checked one. Surprising facts are exactly the ones to check.

cards.hint: Look back at what a good prompt says. And remember: a better prompt doesn't make the answer checked.
cards.explanation: Saying the **goal, context and format** turned 20 paragraphs into 3 useful facts. But a good prompt doesn't make facts true: surprising ones still need **checking** in a trusted source.

cards.title: Give it what it needs
cards.body:
Good prompts can include things you have: **paste in your notes** to summarise, or **your draft** for feedback. You can also ask it to **ask you questions first**, or to **say if it isn't sure**. (It may still be wrong, so you check anyway.)

But never put **private details** in a prompt: your address, passwords, phone number, or anything about friends they haven't agreed to share. Chats may be stored, and you can't always take them back.

cards.prompt: Should each thing go **in** your prompt, or be **left out**?

items.label: How long the answer should be
Your home address, for a local answer
Your school login, to check marks
A friend's private message to you

cards.hint: Ask of each one: does it help the chatbot aim the answer, and is it mine to share?
cards.nudge: Some of these come with a helpful-sounding reason. Is the reason worth sharing something private?
cards.explanation: Who it's for, how long and your own notes help it aim. Your address and login are private even with a good reason (for a local answer, name your town or suburb instead), and a friend's private message isn't yours to share.

cards.prompt: "Give me facts about sharks" got a long, boring list. Which **one** change helps **most**?

options.text: "Give me 3 surprising shark facts for a class talk, one sentence each"

options.nudge: Same prompt, same kind of answer. What did the prompt not say?

options.text: Turn the temperature up as high as it goes
options.nudge: High temperatures add randomness, and nonsense. They don't add what you were missing.

options.text: "Give me facts about sharks, but make them really, really interesting!!!"
options.nudge: That's closer, but how many facts, for what, and how long?

cards.hint: Which option adds a clear goal, context and format?
cards.explanation: Only the first says **how many** (3), **what kind** (surprising), **what for** (a class talk) and **what shape** (one sentence each). "Really, really interesting!!!" is enthusiastic, but still doesn't say what you need.

cards.prompt: You want a chatbot to quiz you on your history notes.

steps.text: You paste your notes and type "Quiz me". It writes 10 questions, with the answers right underneath. What's the best fix?

choices.text: Cover the answers with your hand
choices.consequence: That works a bit, but it's easy to peek, and you didn't fix the prompt.

choices.text: "Ask me one question at a time. Don't show the answer until I reply"
choices.consequence: Now it asks, waits, and tells you if you were right. You said exactly what you wanted.
Harder questions, still with the answers underneath. The prompt didn't say what was wrong.

cards.hint: What exactly went wrong with its answer? Say that in the prompt.
cards.explanation: When an answer isn't what you wanted, **say what was wrong** in the next prompt: here, the format (one question at a time, answers hidden).

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **prompt** works best when it says the **goal**, the **context** and the **format**.
- Specific beats long or polite. If an answer misses, say exactly what was wrong.
- Paste in what you have (notes, drafts), but never private details.
- A better prompt gets a better-aimed answer, not a checked one.

Next: checking AI's work.
